name: mutant-language-tools
description: Language tools for Mutant, powered by a dedicated language server: strict canonical formatting, rich diagnostics (OS-aware platform warnings, unreachable code, unused/undefined/duplicate checks, semicolons), hover with capability categories, completion, semantic highlighting, go-to-definition, references, and rename.

program.description: The .mut source file to debug. Debugging runs from source: a .mu built for release carries no source positions, so there is nothing to step through.

stopOnEntry.description: Stop before the first instruction, so the program can be stepped from the beginning with no breakpoint set.

modulePaths.description: Directories to search for imported modules, in order. The launch configuration's spelling of --module-path.

noDebug.description: Run the program without stopping for anything. Output and the exit code are still reported.

configurationSnippets.label: Mutant: debug the current file
configurationSnippets.description: Compile the open .mut file with positions and debug it.

command.description: gen = compile a .mut to encrypted .mu bytecode; run = execute a compiled .mu; release = build a standalone executable.

src.description: Source (.mut) or bytecode (.mu) file. Defaults to the active editor file.

args.description: Additional raw CLI arguments appended to the command.

mutant.languageServer.path.description: Path or command name for the Mutant language server executable. Leave empty to auto-detect packaged platform binary first, then workspace/PATH.

mutant.languageServer.args.description: Additional command line arguments passed to the Mutant language server.

mutant.cli.path.description: Path or command name for the Mutant CLI, used by the Mutant build/run/release tasks. The CLI is separate from the bundled language server and is expected on PATH by default.

mutant.strictFormatting.description: Format Mutant files using the canonical style: four-space indentation, spaces only, and a semicolon after every statement that requires one. This is a master on/off switch, not a style option — Mutant formatting is deliberately not configurable, so that the same source always produces the same bytes. Set to false to disable Mutant formatting entirely.

mutant.format.onType.enabled.description: Enable on-type formatting for Mutant files. Off by default: on-type formatting reformats the whole document on every ';', '}' and newline, which is disruptive while typing. Format-on-save is enabled by default instead.

mutant.lint.rules.duplicateTopLevelDecla.description: Severity for duplicate top-level declaration lint diagnostics. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.unusedDeclaration.seve.description: Severity for unused top-level declaration lint diagnostics. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.undefinedDeclaration.s.description: Severity for undefined identifier lint diagnostics. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.semicolon.severity.description: Severity for missing or redundant semicolon diagnostics. Both come with a quick fix. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.nestingComplexity.seve.description: Severity for deep nesting diagnostics in function bodies. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.unreachableCode.severi.description: Severity for unreachable-code diagnostics: statements after an unconditional return/break/continue, and a match arm written after `_`, which matches anything. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.platformSupport.severi.description: Severity for platform-support diagnostics: warns when a program calls a builtin that is not supported on the operating system the language server is running on (for example a Windows/Linux-only builtin used on macOS). Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.builtinArity.severity.description: Severity for builtin arity diagnostics: warns when a builtin with a known fixed argument count is called with the wrong number of arguments (for example abs(1, 2) or clamp(x)). Only a curated, verified subset of builtins is checked. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.builtinArgType.severit.description: Severity for builtin argument-type diagnostics: warns when a builtin is passed a value of a type its parameter cannot accept (for example str_upper(42) or len(true)). Only builtins whose parameter types have been verified against their implementation are checked, and only arguments whose type is certain — a literal, or a name that is never reassigned. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.builtinSingleReturn.se.description: Severity for single-return binding diagnostics: warns when several names are bound from a builtin that returns one value rather than a (value, err) pair (for example let updated, err = push(items, x)). Nothing fails at runtime — if the value is an array the binding takes it apart, and otherwise the extra names are always null, so an if (err) check never fires. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.builtinPairReturn.seve.description: Severity for pair-return binding diagnostics: warns when one name is bound from a builtin that returns a (value, err) pair (for example let data = fs_read(path)). The name holds the pair rather than the value, and nothing fails at the binding — a pair prints as its value, so the mistake surfaces somewhere else or not at all. Silent when the program does something with the name that only makes sense for a pair, such as indexing it or returning it. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.builtinDeprecated.seve.description: Severity for deprecated-builtin diagnostics: reports a call to a builtin that is kept only so existing programs keep working, and names its replacement (for example net_syn_scan, replaced by net_connect_scan). The call is correct and still runs, which is why this defaults to a hint rather than a warning. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.spawnGlobalWrite.sever.description: Severity for spawned-callback global-write diagnostics: warns when a spawn, pmap or peach callback assigns to a top-level name. Those callbacks run on their own VM with a snapshot of the globals, so the write lands in a copy that is discarded when the callback finishes — the program runs, reports nothing, and the value never changes. Only a function literal written at the call site is checked, and only a name the callback does not rebind for itself. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.unclosedResource.sever.description: Severity for unclosed-resource diagnostics: warns when a builtin that opens a handle (ntfs_open, zip_open, chan_new, net_connect and their families) binds it to a name nothing in the same scope closes. Handles live in a package-level store with no eviction, so an unclosed one is held for the life of the process — invisible in a script that exits, descriptor exhaustion in a loop or a long-running server. The rule stays quiet whenever the handle is used somewhere it cannot follow (returned, passed to a helper, stored) or the closer is named anywhere in the scope, including inside with_resource. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.uncheckedError.severit.description: Severity for unchecked-error diagnostics: warns when `let value, err = f(...)` binds the error half of a (value, err) builtin and nothing reads that binding before the name is rebound or the scope ends. A failed call leaves null in the value beside the error, so a program that ignores the error carries on with nothing and reports success. The rule stays quiet when the error is read in any way at all — tested, printed, returned, passed on — when the failure is caught through the value instead (an `if` or `for` condition on it, or a BOOLEAN success flag used anywhere), when a nested function mentions the name, and when `_` is bound to say the failure is deliberately ignored. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

mutant.lint.rules.matchExhaustiveness.se.description: Severity for match-exhaustiveness diagnostics: warns when every arm of a match is a variant of one enum declared in the same file, no arm is `_`, and a variant of that enum has no arm. A match must produce a value, so a subject no arm matches raises at run time rather than yielding null — which means adding a variant to an enum silently leaves every existing match over it one arm short. The rule stays quiet unless it is certain: a literal pattern, two different enums, an imported enum (`mod.Status.Ok`, whose variants live in another file), a `_` arm, or a name that is both an enum and a `let` binding all suppress it. Set to 'off' to suppress the rule.

scripts.pretest: npm run compile-tests && npm run lint
